newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MITI deregulation to target power utilities.
newsitem.headline: Japan MITI deregulation to target power utilities.

text.p: Japan's trade ministry will unveil a broad package of deregulation measures on Friday aimed at stirring up competition within the heavily insulated power utilities industry.

The Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) is expected to release details of an action programme reviewing a wide range of industrial sectors, including telecommunications and distribution.
But electric power companies, perhaps the most blaring example over government protection, were expected to absorb the lion's share of the shock.
"Without doubt, a major aim of the action programme is to reform the electric power industry," a MITI official close to finalising the action programme said.

Officials declined to reveal details of the programme ahead of the official announcement but said the plan will include recommendations to improve power plant operating rates, promote the independent power producer (IPP) scheme, and review the current system of generating and distributing power.
The programme's wide-ranging review will attempt to slash Japan's high electricity rates to levels comparable to those overseas by 2001, a goal pledged by the government last year.
"Our objective is to create a competitive market (in the electric power utilities industry)," another MITI official said.
Japan has 10 private electric power companies, each of which enjoys a regional monopoly in exchange for providing a stable supply of electricity.
Industry analysts said the upcoming programme is also likely to recommend the introduction of a competitive bidding system for the construction of new thermal power plants.

Thermal power -- which includes energy sources such as crude oil, coal and liquefied natural gas (LNG) -- accounted for 56.1 percent of electricity generated in the past fiscal year which ended March 31.
Analysts said the bidding will almost certainly be opened to foreign companies as well as Japanese companies.
"I don't think they have a choice, I think they will have to open (competitive bidding) to foreign companies," said Tadatoshi Utaka of Japan's Nikko Research Centre.
The programme will also seek to improve transparency in the industry's costs by introducing a separate accounting system for generating and distribution expenditures, analysts said.
Industry analysts said a separate accounting system would help promote the fledgling IPP scheme, the wholesale electricity business first introduced in Japan in the last 1996/97 business year.

In the first year, Japan's electric power companies awarded tenders amounting to roughly three million kilowatts (kw) to the independent producers, which will begin supplying electricity as soon as 1999.
The figure represents a tiny percentage of the total amount of power consumed in Japan, which amounted to 775.4 billion kilowatt hours (kWh) last year.
But MITI believes that IPPs will stimulate competition in the electric power industry.
Ahead of the release of the action programme, Tokyo Electric Power Co Inc (TEPCO) last week announced that it planned to cut electricity rates early next year.
A handful of electric power utilities have followed suit with similar announcements, but none of the firms, including TEPCO, have said how much their rates would be cut.
